title: Overview of research progress and application of experimental models of colorectal cancer

subsections.subsection_title: Established 2D Cell Line Models and Their Molecular Characterization
subsections.content:
Established two-dimensional (2D) cell line models remain foundational tools in colorectal cancer (CRC) research due to their reproducibility, ease of manipulation, and compatibility with high-throughput assays. Comprehensive molecular characterization of these lines has revealed their capacity to recapitulate key genetic and epigenetic features of primary tumors, including chromosomal instability (CIN), microsatellite instability (MSI), and the CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP). A landmark study profiling 24 colon cancer cell lines confirmed that 20 out of 24 harbored mutually exclusive activating mutations in KRAS or BRAF, while 13 exhibited PIK3CA or PTEN alterations, leading to PI3K/AKT pathway hyperactivation; notably, four lines lacked mutations in these canonical drivers, highlighting molecular heterogeneity ref [1]. Furthermore, MSI was detected in nine lines, and CIMP status varied depending on the epimarker panel used, with the Weisenberger panel demonstrating superior discriminatory power ref [1]. These findings align with broader classifications of CRC molecular subtypes, where cell lines faithfully mirror the Wnt, MAPK, p53, TGFβ, and PI3K pathway alterations observed in vivo ref [3].

Recent efforts have expanded the repertoire of well-characterized models by introducing low-passage cell lines derived from clinically annotated tumors, which better preserve the phenotypic and genetic diversity of primary CRCs. These novel lines exhibit heterogeneous epithelial-mesenchymal features, including E-cadherin mutations and β-catenin stabilization, mirroring in vivo tumor evolution ref [4]. Such models enhance translational relevance by capturing subtypes not fully represented in traditional, long-passaged lines. Molecular authentication via short tandem repeat profiling and comprehensive mutational screening is now considered essential to ensure model fidelity and experimental reproducibility ref [1]. The availability of annotated panels, such as those detailing CIN, MSI, and CIMP status, enables researchers to select cell lines tailored to specific biological questions, from signaling pathway analysis to drug response profiling ref [3].

subsections.subsection_title: Cancer Stem Cells and Tumor Aggressiveness in Experimental Models
subsections.content:
Cancer stem cells (CSCs) play a pivotal role in driving tumor aggressiveness, chemoresistance, and recurrence in colorectal cancer (CRC). The identification of CD133 as a marker for tumorigenic colon cancer cells established a foundational model for isolating CSCs capable of initiating and propagating tumors in immunodeficient mice, with these cells maintaining their phenotype across serial transplants ref [4]. Beyond surface markers, transcriptional regulators such as SOX2 have been shown to enhance CSC properties by activating β-catenin and Beclin1-mediated autophagy, thereby promoting epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and chemoresistance through ABCC2 upregulation ref [5]. Hypoxic tumor microenvironments further amplify CSC-driven aggressiveness; CSN8 has emerged as a critical regulator that stabilizes HIF-1α under low oxygen, inducing EMT, dormancy, and survival under stress conditions such as chemotherapy or serum deprivation ref [4]. These mechanisms collectively enable CSCs to evade therapy and seed metastatic niches. Experimental models incorporating hypoxia, 3D culture, and patient-derived xenografts have revealed that CSCs exhibit dynamic plasticity, adapting their phenotype in response to microenvironmental cues. Targeting CSC-specific pathways—such as SOX2/β-catenin or CSN8/HIF-1α—represents a promising strategy to disrupt tumor maintenance and prevent relapse in CRC.

Recent advances in experimental models have enabled the functional dissection of CSC heterogeneity and their interactions with stromal components, highlighting the need for physiologically relevant systems that recapitulate the dynamic tumor niche. Combining lineage tracing, single-cell RNA sequencing, and in vivo imaging in CSC-enriched models is now uncovering novel vulnerabilities that could be exploited therapeutically.

subsections.subsection_title: Three-Dimensional Models: Spheroids and Organoids in Colorectal Cancer Research
subsections.content:
Three-dimensional (3D) models have emerged as critical tools for recapitulating the architectural and functional complexity of colorectal cancer (CRC) beyond traditional 2D monolayers. Multicellular tumor spheroids, generated through suspension culture or microfabricated platforms, mimic key tumor microenvironmental features such as oxygen and nutrient gradients, leading to stratified zones of proliferation, quiescence, and necrosis—mirroring in vivo solid tumors ref [7]. Recent advances in high-throughput spheroid generation, including centrifugation-based methods in poly-HEMA-coated plates, enable standardized, reproducible models suitable for drug screening and toxicity assessment ref [10]. Ex vivo-derived colospheres, established directly from patient tumor tissues, preserve tumor heterogeneity and aggressive phenotypes, offering a clinically relevant platform to study invasion and chemoresistance ref [9].

Organoids, derived from patient-derived stem cells or tumor biopsies, represent a more sophisticated 3D model by self-organizing into crypt-villus structures that recapitulate the cellular diversity and polarity of the colonic epithelium ref [7]. These organoids maintain genetic and phenotypic stability over long-term culture, enabling modeling of tumor initiation, progression, and response to targeted therapies in a patient-specific context. Their utility extends to co-culture systems incorporating stromal and immune cells, thereby better simulating the tumor microenvironment ref [11]. Together, spheroids and organoids bridge the gap between conventional cell lines and in vivo models, offering enhanced predictive power for preclinical drug testing and personalized medicine approaches in colorectal cancer research.

subsections.subsection_title: Chemically Induced Animal Models of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.content:
Chemically induced animal models have long served as foundational tools for studying colorectal cancer (CRC) pathogenesis, particularly in elucidating the role of environmental and dietary factors in tumorigenesis. The azoxymethane (AOM) and 1,2-dimethylhydrazine (DMH) protocols, which induce DNA alkylation and subsequent mutations in colonic epithelial cells, remain the most widely used methods to generate tumors resembling human CRC in rodents. These models reliably produce adenocarcinomas with histopathological and molecular features akin to human disease, including APC, KRAS, and p53 mutations. Notably, dietary interventions have been shown to modulate tumor development in these systems; for instance, dietary wheat bran and dehydrated citrus fiber significantly reduce tumor incidence and multiplicity in F344 rats exposed to 3,2'-dimethyl-4-aminobiphenyl (DMAB), highlighting the protective role of specific fiber types against chemical carcinogenesis ref [12].

Beyond fiber, other modulators such as bile acids, high-fat diets, and anti-inflammatory agents have been tested in chemically induced models to dissect gene-environment interactions. The combination of AOM with dextran sodium sulfate (DSS) has further enabled the modeling of inflammation-associated CRC, mimicking the colitis-associated cancer pathway. These models have been instrumental in validating chemopreventive agents and identifying early biomarkers of neoplastic transformation. While limitations include species-specific metabolic differences and the absence of spontaneous tumor progression seen in genetic models, chemically induced systems offer high reproducibility, cost-effectiveness, and temporal control over tumor initiation, making them indispensable for preclinical screening and mechanistic studies.

Xenograft and heterotransplantation models have played a pivotal role in colorectal cancer (CRC) research by enabling the direct study of human tumor biology in immunodeficient hosts. The foundational breakthrough came with the successful engraftment of a human colonic adenocarcinoma into nude mice, which lack a functional thymus and T-cell-mediated immunity, thereby overcoming the immune rejection barrier that had previously thwarted human tumor transplantation efforts ref [13]. This seminal work demonstrated that human CRC tissues could retain their histological and molecular characteristics in vivo, paving the way for serial passaging and preclinical drug testing. Subsequent refinements led to the development of more severely immunocompromised strains, such as NOD/SCID and NSG mice, which support higher engraftment rates and better preservation of tumor heterogeneity.

Patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) now represent a gold standard for modeling CRC progression and therapy response, as they maintain the genetic, phenotypic, and stromal complexity of the original tumor better than cell line-based models. PDX models have been instrumental in identifying biomarkers of drug resistance, evaluating targeted therapies, and personalizing treatment strategies. However, limitations persist, including the absence of a fully reconstituted human immune microenvironment and the time and cost associated with engraftment and expansion. Recent efforts to humanize these models with immune components aim to bridge this gap and enhance translational relevance.

subsections.subsection_title: Genetic Models and Molecular Pathways in CRC
subsections.content:
Genetic models of colorectal cancer (CRC) have been instrumental in elucidating the molecular pathways driving tumorigenesis, particularly through the dysregulation of key genes such as APC, KRAS, TP53, and mismatch repair (MMR) components. The APC gene, a central regulator of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, is frequently inactivated in both sporadic and hereditary CRC. Studies have demonstrated that somatic APC mutations occur in over 50% of HNPCC cases, with a predominance of frameshift mutations at mononucleotide repeats, suggesting a strong link to MMR deficiency as an early driver event ref [14]. Mouse models with germline Apc mutations, such as the ApcMin/+ strain, recapitulate intestinal polyposis and have been pivotal in validating the adenoma-carcinoma sequence. Combinatorial genetic models, including Apc/Trp53 and Apc/Kras mutants, have further revealed cooperative oncogenic interactions that accelerate tumor progression and metastasis. Additionally, models with conditional knockout of MMR genes (e.g., Msh2, Mlh1) have mirrored the microsatellite instability phenotype observed in Lynch syndrome, enabling studies on immune evasion and therapeutic response. These models collectively underscore the centrality of Wnt signaling, genomic instability, and clonal evolution in CRC pathogenesis.

Beyond canonical pathways, emerging genetic models have integrated CRISPR-Cas9-mediated editing to introduce patient-specific mutations into organoid systems, bridging in vivo genetics with human tumor biology. Such approaches facilitate functional validation of driver mutations in defined genetic backgrounds and improve the predictive power of preclinical testing.

Patient-derived organoid (PDO) models have emerged as transformative tools in colorectal cancer (CRC) research, offering a physiologically relevant platform that preserves the genetic, phenotypic, and functional heterogeneity of original tumors. These 3D cultures, derived directly from patient tumor tissues, maintain key molecular features including somatic mutations and copy number alterations, enabling accurate recapitulation of tumor biology in vitro. The prospective generation of a living organoid biobank from CRC patients has demonstrated that tumor organoids faithfully mirror the mutational spectra of their parental tumors, facilitating high-throughput drug screening and the identification of gene-drug associations for personalized therapy ref [15].

Critically, PDOs have shown remarkable predictive power in modeling clinical treatment responses. In a landmark study, organoids derived from metastatic gastrointestinal cancers accurately reflected individual patient responses to chemotherapy and targeted agents, outperforming traditional xenograft models in correlating ex vivo drug sensitivity with clinical outcomes ref [16]. This capability positions PDOs as viable tools for guiding precision oncology, particularly in heavily pretreated patients where conventional models fail. Moreover, PDOs can be co-cultured with immune cells and stromal components to investigate tumor-microenvironment interactions, further enhancing their translational utility.

subsections.subsection_title: Modeling Tumor Initiation and Progression in Colorectal Cancer
subsections.content:
Modeling tumor initiation and progression in colorectal cancer (CRC) requires systems that recapitulate the stepwise accumulation of genetic and epigenetic alterations driving malignant transformation. Recent advances have integrated organoid models with CRISPR-mediated gene editing to introduce canonical drivers such as APC, KRAS, and TP53 mutations, enabling precise dissection of early tumorigenic events in human colonic epithelium. These models faithfully mirror the histopathological and molecular heterogeneity observed in patient tumors, including the emergence of cancer stem cell populations and epithelial-mesenchymal transition dynamics. The conceptual framework of cancer hallmarks, recently expanded to include cellular plasticity, epigenetic reprogramming, and microbiome interactions, provides a critical lens for interpreting these models ref [17]. For instance, epigenetic dysregulation in CRC initiation has been modeled using organoids exposed to inflammatory cytokines or microbial metabolites, revealing how microenvironmental cues cooperate with somatic mutations to accelerate neoplasia. Additionally, xenotransplantation of genetically engineered organoids into immunodeficient mice allows longitudinal tracking of tumor progression and metastatic dissemination in vivo. The integration of single-cell omics with these models further uncovers clonal evolution patterns and resistance mechanisms emerging during tumor advancement.

Collectively, these experimental systems bridge the gap between traditional cell lines and patient-derived tissues, offering unprecedented resolution for studying CRC pathogenesis from initiation to advanced disease. Their utility extends to testing targeted interventions against emerging hallmarks, such as metabolic reprogramming and neuronal crosstalk, thereby informing precision oncology strategies.

Chemical-induced models of colorectal cancer have long served as critical tools for elucidating environmental contributions to tumorigenesis, particularly through dietary carcinogens. Among the most extensively studied are heterocyclic amines (HCAs) formed during high-temperature cooking of meat and fish. 2-Amino-1-methyl-6-phenylimidazo[4,5-b]pyridine (PhIP), identified as the most abundant HCA in cooked proteins, reliably induces colon and mammary carcinomas in F344 rats when administered in the diet, making it a cornerstone model for diet-related CRC research ref [2]. PhIP’s metabolic activation by cytochrome P450 enzymes and subsequent DNA adduct formation in colonic epithelium mirrors key molecular events in human sporadic CRC, providing a physiologically relevant platform for studying initiation and promotion phases.

Beyond PhIP, other chemical agents such as azoxymethane (AOM) and 1,2-dimethylhydrazine (DMH) have been widely employed to induce colonic aberrant crypt foci (ACF) and adenocarcinomas in rodents, often in combination with inflammatory stimuli to model colitis-associated cancer ref [3]. These models recapitulate the adenoma-carcinoma sequence and allow for temporal analysis of molecular alterations, including mutations in APC, KRAS, and p53. More recently, combinations of chemical carcinogens with high-fat diets have been used to investigate metabolic influences on tumor progression, enhancing translational relevance to human obesity-linked CRC. The reproducibility, cost-effectiveness, and histopathological fidelity of chemical models continue to support their utility in preclinical drug screening and mechanistic studies.

subsections.subsection_title: Genetic Drivers in Early Colorectal Carcinogenesis
subsections.content:
Genetic drivers play a pivotal role in the initiation of colorectal carcinogenesis, with mutations in key oncogenes and tumor suppressors occurring in early precancerous lesions. Oncogenic K-ras mutations, detected in aberrant crypt foci (ACF), are among the earliest molecular events in colon tumorigenesis, driving epithelial transformation in a location-dependent manner. In transgenic mouse models, K-ras^G12D activation in the proximal colon induces ACF with high progression potential, characterized by upregulation of PKCβII and sustained MEK/ERK signaling, whereas distal ACF exhibit apoptosis and limited neoplastic progression, highlighting regional heterogeneity in oncogenic response ref [19]. Beyond K-ras, APC loss remains the most common initiating event in sporadic and familial adenomatous polyposis, leading to β-catenin stabilization and Wnt pathway hyperactivation ref [16]. Somatic mutations in TP53 and PIK3CA also emerge in early adenomas, contributing to evasion of apoptosis and enhanced survival. Recent studies using lineage tracing in murine models demonstrate that colonic stem cells are the primary cellular targets for these initiating mutations, with their clonal expansion forming the foundation of adenoma development. The interplay between genetic alterations and the local microenvironment further modulates lesion fate, underscoring the complexity of early carcinogenic events.

Emerging evidence implicates additional drivers such as BRAF V600E, particularly in serrated pathway tumors, and mutations in RNF43, which disrupt Wnt regulation in microsatellite-unstable lesions. The temporal sequence of these mutations, often revealed through next-generation sequencing of microdissected ACF and adenomas, supports a stepwise model of carcinogenesis. Mouse models combining conditional alleles of APC, K-ras, and TP53 have enabled dissection of cooperative interactions, revealing that K-ras activation accelerates tumorigenesis in APC-deficient backgrounds. These findings reinforce the notion that early genetic events are not merely initiators but also shape the molecular subtype and clinical trajectory of subsequent tumors.

subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Models of Colorectal Cancer Initiation and Progression
subsections.content:
Experimental models of colorectal cancer (CRC) initiation and progression have evolved to recapitulate the stepwise accumulation of genetic alterations driving tumorigenesis. Transgenic mouse models expressing oncogenic K-ras mutations, such as K-ras^{G12D}, have demonstrated that this mutation is a critical early event in colonic neoplasia, inducing aberrant crypt foci (ACF) morphologically identical to those induced by chemical carcinogens like azoxymethane (AOM). Notably, the spatial context of K-ras activation dictates phenotypic outcomes: proximal colon lesions exhibit sustained proliferation and PKCβII upregulation, enabling progression to dysplastic microadenomas, whereas distal lesions undergo apoptosis and remain indolent, highlighting regional heterogeneity in carcinogenic susceptibility. Complementary models incorporating Apc loss, either alone or in combination with K-ras activation, have further delineated the cooperative roles of Wnt and MAPK signaling in adenoma formation and malignant conversion. Patient-derived xenografts and organoid systems derived from early-stage lesions now enable longitudinal tracking of clonal evolution and microenvironmental interactions during tumor initiation. Additionally, chemically induced models using agents such as 1,2-dimethylhydrazine or PhIP provide robust platforms for studying environmental contributions to CRC initiation, particularly in the context of diet and gut microbiota modulation.

Recent advances have integrated CRISPR-Cas9-mediated somatic mutagenesis into intestinal organoids, allowing precise modeling of sequential mutations (e.g., APC, KRAS, TP53) in a human epithelial context. These systems, when transplanted into immunodeficient mice, faithfully reproduce the histopathological and molecular progression from adenoma to invasive carcinoma, offering a human-relevant platform for mechanistic and therapeutic studies.

subsections.subsection_title: Metabolic Reprogramming in CRC Experimental Models
subsections.content:
Metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of colorectal cancer (CRC), with altered glycolysis, glutaminolysis, and lipid metabolism driving tumor growth and therapy resistance. Experimental models have been instrumental in elucidating these metabolic shifts, particularly the overexpression of hexokinase 2 (HK2), which enhances glucose uptake and lactate production in CRC cells. Ref [1] demonstrated that xanthohumol suppresses CRC proliferation in vitro and in vivo by downregulating HK2-mediated glycolysis, concurrently activating the intrinsic apoptotic pathway via cytochrome c release. This effect was mediated through inhibition of the EGFR-Akt signaling axis, highlighting a key regulatory node in CRC metabolic adaptation. Beyond glycolysis, CRC models have revealed increased glutamine dependency, with glutaminase inhibitors showing efficacy in patient-derived xenografts and organoid systems. Lipid metabolism is also rewired, with fatty acid synthase (FASN) upregulation promoting membrane biosynthesis and signaling in CRC cell lines. Recent studies using isotope tracing in 3D organoid cultures have uncovered compartment-specific metabolic heterogeneity, mirroring in vivo tumor microenvironments. Additionally, hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) modulate metabolic enzyme expression in CRC models, linking oxygen tension to glycolytic flux and chemoresistance.

Emerging microphysiological systems, including perfused organ-on-a-chip platforms, now enable real-time monitoring of metabolic dynamics under controlled nutrient and oxygen gradients, offering unprecedented resolution for studying metabolic crosstalk between tumor and stromal cells. These models are critical for evaluating metabolic inhibitors in physiologically relevant contexts, bridging the gap between traditional 2D cultures and in vivo studies.

subsections.subsection_title: Epigenetic and Molecular Characterization of CRC Cell Lines and Tumors
subsections.content:
Epigenetic and molecular characterization of colorectal cancer (CRC) cell lines and tumors has been pivotal in elucidating the heterogeneity and drivers of disease progression. Landmark studies have demonstrated that promoter hypermethylation of tumor suppressor genes, including hMLH1, MGMT, p16INK4a, and E-cadherin, is prevalent in both primary CRCs and their derived cell lines, with distinct patterns observed between microsatellite stable (MSS) and unstable (MSI) subtypes ref [21]. These epigenetic alterations often correlate with mutation profiles of APC, KRAS, and TP53, underscoring the interplay between genetic and epigenetic events in CRC pathogenesis. Comparative analyses have revealed that while cell lines retain key molecular features of their parental tumors, they also acquire culture-induced epigenetic drift, necessitating careful validation for translational relevance. Recent high-throughput profiling has expanded this landscape, identifying novel methylated loci and non-coding RNA regulators that distinguish molecular subtypes, including CMS1–4 classifications. Furthermore, integrated multi-omics approaches have linked DNA methylation signatures to chromatin accessibility and histone modification patterns, providing mechanistic insights into transcriptional dysregulation in CRC.

The utility of cell lines as models is further refined by their molecular annotation, enabling subtype-specific drug screening and resistance studies. However, discrepancies between cell line epigenomes and primary tumor profiles highlight the need for patient-derived models, such as organoids, to preserve in vivo epigenetic fidelity. Ongoing efforts to standardize molecular characterization protocols and establish reference epigenomes for CRC models are critical for improving reproducibility and clinical predictability in preclinical research.

subsections.subsection_title: In Vitro and Microphysiological Systems for CRC Metastasis and Tissue Modeling
subsections.content:
In vitro and microphysiological systems have emerged as powerful tools for modeling colorectal cancer (CRC) metastasis and tissue architecture with enhanced physiological relevance. Recent advances in microfluidic platforms now enable the co-culture of CRC organoids with secondary organ constructs, recapitulating the multi-step metastatic cascade. For instance, a multi-site metastasis-on-a-chip system has been developed to simultaneously house primary CRC organoids alongside liver, lung, and endothelial microtissues under recirculating flow, allowing real-time tracking of circulating tumor cells and organ-specific colonization preferences ref [22]. These systems integrate extracellular matrix-derived hydrogels and photopatterning techniques to preserve tumor-stroma interactions critical for metastatic behavior. Beyond single-organ models, organ-on-a-chip platforms incorporating immune cells and biomechanical cues have improved the fidelity of metastatic niche modeling, enabling studies of extravasation, dormancy, and outgrowth in a controlled microenvironment.

Complementary advances include 3D bioprinted CRC models that mimic vascularized tumor microenvironments and patient-derived organoid co-cultures integrated with perfusable vasculature, enhancing predictive power for therapeutic response. Such systems bridge the gap between conventional 2D cultures and in vivo models, offering high-throughput, human-relevant platforms for mechanistic studies of metastatic tropism and drug resistance. The integration of real-time imaging, biosensors, and single-cell omics further empowers dynamic analysis of metastatic progression within engineered tissue contexts.

subsections.subsection_title: Preclinical Models for CRC Therapeutic Response and Resistance
subsections.content:
Preclinical models for evaluating therapeutic response and resistance in colorectal cancer (CRC) have evolved from simple cell line xenografts to more sophisticated systems that better recapitulate tumor heterogeneity and microenvironmental influences. Cell line-based platforms, such as the NCI-60 panel, remain foundational for high-throughput drug screening and biomarker discovery, enabling systematic correlation of genomic profiles with drug sensitivity ref [23]. However, their limited physiological relevance has spurred the adoption of patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) and organoids, which preserve the genetic and phenotypic diversity of primary tumors and better predict clinical outcomes ref [16]. Recent studies have highlighted the role of therapy-induced senescence as a resistance mechanism; for instance, irinotecan treatment in CRC models activates Akt as a feedback survival signal, and its inhibition shifts the cellular response from senescence to apoptosis, thereby enhancing therapeutic efficacy and reducing emergent resistant clones ref [24]. These findings underscore the importance of modeling dynamic adaptive responses, not just static drug sensitivity.

Emerging microphysiological systems, including organoid-co-culture platforms and tumor-on-a-chip devices, now enable real-time monitoring of resistance development under controlled microenvironments, integrating stromal and immune components. Such models facilitate the dissection of molecular mechanisms underlying acquired resistance, such as epigenetic reprogramming or metabolic adaptation, and allow for combinatorial drug testing in a more clinically relevant context. While no single model fully captures human tumor complexity, the strategic integration of cell lines, PDXs, organoids, and engineered systems offers a tiered approach to deconvoluting therapeutic resistance and accelerating precision oncology.
